title: ORDER BY in Postgres can return a different row order than the exact same query on a different server
assumption: ORDER BY on a text column is a property of the SQL and the data, so the same query against the same rows always returns the same order.

input.display: SELECT name FROM users ORDER BY name;
input.description: A plain text ORDER BY on a column using the database's default collation, run against two Postgres instances whose cluster was initialized with different default collations (e.g. "C" vs "en_US.utf8" vs an ICU collation).

what_goes_wrong: The identical query on identical rows returns a different order on a database whose collation is "C" (byte order: case-sensitive, uppercase before lowercase, accented letters after z) than on one using an "en_US" libc or ICU collation (a, ä, Z interleaved by letter). Restoring or migrating into a database with a different default collation, or upgrading the operating system's locale data under the same collation name, can change ORDER BY results without changing a row of data or a line of SQL.
why: Postgres orders text using a collation. Each text column has one, which defaults to the database's collation, and a query can override it with COLLATE. The database default is fixed when the database is created, and the actual ordering comes from either the C library's locale data (the libc provider) or ICU (supported since PostgreSQL 10). So the same SQL orders differently in databases with different collations, and even the same collation name, such as en_US.utf8, can order differently after an operating-system upgrade changes the C library's locale data (the glibc 2.28 change is the best-known case, and it also left existing text indexes inconsistent). A pg_dump made without --create does not carry the database's default collation, so restoring it into a database created with a different default changes every un-pinned text sort.

repros.note: SELECT name FROM (VALUES ('a'),('Z'),('ä')) AS t(name) ORDER BY name COLLATE "C"; returns Z, a, ä (UTF-8 byte order, matching the plain code-point sorts in the Python/JS repros above). The same query with COLLATE "en-US-x-icu" (available when PostgreSQL is built with ICU) returns a, ä, Z, matching the localeCompare repro above. Without a COLLATE clause the result depends on the database's collation, which you can see with SELECT datcollate FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database();

fix: Pin collation explicitly with COLLATE in any ORDER BY whose result order matters across environments (tests comparing row order, pagination cursors, anything exported and diffed). Check the database collation with SELECT datcollate FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database();. Treat a restore onto a server with different locale or ICU data, or an OS upgrade that changes glibc, as a behaviour change for every un-pinned text sort, and reindex text indexes after such an upgrade.
